title: Old-time diseases and ailments; definitions of ague, quinsy, felons, carbuncles, and the itch
description: Clara Grove introduces the topic of old-time farmer remedies and the diseases they treated. She defines several outdated ailments including ague, quinsy, felons, carbuncles, and the itch, explaining their symptoms and how they were treated.

title: Herbal medicine; missionary cure story; specific herbs and their uses
description: Grove recounts the story of a missionary's wife who was cured by Indian herbal medicine after American doctors failed. She then discusses various herbs used as medicine, including sage, hops for flu, peppermint, sassafras, wild cherry bark, licorice, rhubarb, and catnip.

title: Frontier medical care; distance from doctors; house calls and costs
description: The conversation turns to the reality of frontier medicine, where doctors might be 50 to 100 miles away. Grove explains how people treated themselves with cherry bark tea and other remedies, discusses the cost of house calls, and contrasts old practices with modern medicine.

title: Poultices, plasters, and external remedies; onion poultices; turpentine stupes; mustard plasters
description: Grove describes external treatments including witch hazel for aches, onion poultices for pneumonia, turpentine stupes, and mustard plasters. She shares a story about saving a boy with an onion poultice and explains how to prepare these treatments.

title: Household remedies; hot salt bags; ginger tea; bloodletting; conclusion
description: The final section covers various household remedies including hot black coffee for headaches, hot salt bags as heating pads, ginger tea, and the folk cure of wrapping a stocking around the neck for sore throat. Grove also mentions the old practice of bloodletting and concludes by noting how self-reliant people had to be when living far from doctors.
